Hi Richard,
Just to be sure and to ask a pertinent question: Do I make predictions
based on my best model (not all the p-values are < 0.05) or based on a
model containing only significant covariates?
For detection, only three covariates have a significant effect: visit
(like you programm it: 1, 2, 3 or4) (sampling covariate), nesting type
(two dummy variables) and hour of the day (from 0 to 10; sampling

appendData=TRUE)

0

0

appendData=TRUE)

So, my questions are:
- Do I make predictions based on my best model (not all the p-values
are < 0.05) or based on a model containing only significant
covariates?

day being a sampling covariate and ranging from 0 to 10)?

Aude

messages.author: 057bfe4d4b636b43
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Predicting p
parts:
Hi Aude,

1) Selection of a "best model" model is often very subjective, even using AIC. Usually models are thrown out if parameters don't converge, if additional parameters don't seem to be adding things etc. If your "AIC best model" is getting a lot of weight and the parameters converge you'd at least have some justification to use it. Just be aware that and AIC table isn't as cut and dry of a model selection criteria as is often advertised. If there is a lot of ambiguity, may want to model average (see examples at the bottom of ?fitList) .
2) If you look at detection1, it should have 4 rows. Predict will generate a prediction for each unique row of covariates
3) For detection2, it looks like visit has length 4, but hour has length of 942, under a data.frame, this won't do. What exactly are you trying to do?
4) I am running a suite of 257 models (bad, I know), but the modSel and prediction on this suite can take a very, very long time (well more than an hour, on a fairly high end machine).


Matthew

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Predicting p
parts:
Hi Aude,

In general, if there is nothing weird with your AIC best model (that is, all parameters were estimable, no parameters have infinite variance), the decision to use a model with deltaAIC>20 is very defensible, especially within the wildlife community. In general, the IC folk kind of frown on p-value approaches.

So, hour of day is in the best model for occupancy, but not for detection, is that right? Quick question, the model says visit number effects detection probability as well as time of day. Does this make sense? I notice in your predictions that the detection probability declines as a function of visit, does this suggest that you have animals that are "trap responding?" 

So, if you have 942 hour of day measurements, do you want one visit for each measurement? (4 X 942? ) If this is the case, the expand.grid function may do what you want. For instance

detection2 = expand.grid(Visit=1:4,Hours=seq(0,9.42,by=0.01),nesting1=0,nesting2=0).

Feeding detection2 above through your statements should give a prediction for every combination of Visit and Hour with nesting1=0 and nesting2=0.

In terms of the prediction not working, I don't know on that one. I find unmarked to be pretty fast, at least compared to Bayesian estimation I'm certainly not going to complain about how long it takes to get a parameter estimates. If the above doesn't work maybe provide the code you are using and first 5 rows of data?

Matthew

Hi Matthew,
To return to model selection, my best model contains 18 covariates for
psi and 16 covariates for p. I use p-values of the output to determine
which covariates have a significant effect. Example for psi:
Estimate SE z p(>z)
Elevation -0.3312 0.10 -1.58 0.1138
Distance road 0.4205 0.15 2.80 0.0050
Date 3.7473 1.4 2.68 0.0074

From this, I obtain: p~nesting type+hour of the day+visit and
psi~distance to the nearest road+date. For us, it makes sense that
detection decreases with the visit number because we used mobbing
calls playback to attract birds and we observed a habituation
phenomenon. Also, we noticed that we observed more birds in the middle
of the morning compared to the beginning and the end of this period.
The code you gave me works. After calculating these predictions, I
merge the results with my data to obtain predictions for my
observations.
Thank you for your help and have a nice day,
Aude
